text: Driftwood's raw billing data includes subscriber email addresses -- genuine PII that most people with access to this platform have no legitimate reason to see in plain text. This lesson applies the Snowflake course's own RBAC and masking lessons to that real column.

Three roles, least-privilege. DRIFTWOOD_TRANSFORMER, the dbt and Airflow service account, sees email in plain text because it needs to, to build the pipeline. DRIFTWOOD_ANALYST, human analysts and Power BI's own service account, sees email masked. DRIFTWOOD_COMPLIANCE, a small group with a real, specific need -- like a data-deletion request -- sees it unmasked.
This mirrors Snowflake's own real role hierarchy and switch-role mechanism -- each role scoped to exactly what its function requires, never broad access granted out of convenience.

The masking policy itself is a CASE statement keyed on CURRENT_ROLE(). Compliance and the transformer see the real address; every other role, including the analyst role Power BI connects as, sees a redacted version -- the stored value never changes, only what the query returns.
Here's the real mechanism unmasked -- a table queried with no masking policy applied, showing the actual underlying values.
The identical table, queried by a lower-privileged role once the masking policy is active -- same rows, same query, genuinely different result, enforced at query time.

A simpler option -- just don't grant the analyst role any access to the email column at all -- would also protect the data, but breaks differently and worse. A report running SELECT star would error out entirely. Masking lets the column exist in every result set while the sensitive value itself stays hidden -- a dashboard that keeps working beats a query that breaks loudly.
Next lesson: CI/CD for the dbt project -- testing every change before it ever reaches this same production data.
